parts.label: (a)
parts.text: For a progressive wave, state what is meant by the frequency.

markscheme_points.text: number of oscillations per unit time (of source / point on wave / particle) / wavefronts / crests / troughs passing a fixed point per unit time

hints: Hint 1: Think about what is actually vibrating in a sound wave - the source and the air particles - and what you would count if you watched one particle for one second.
parts.proper_answer: Frequency is the number of oscillations per unit time of a particle in the wave, equal to the number of wavefronts passing a fixed point per unit time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture one particle**
Imagine sitting beside one tiny bit of air as the sound passes. It moves back and forth about its equilibrium position. Frequency tells you how fast that to-and-fro repeats.

Step 2: **Link to the passing wave**
For a progressive wave each oscillation of the source sends out one wavelength. So counting oscillations in one second is the same as counting how many crests or compressions sweep past you in one second. That is $f$ in $\text{Hz}$ or $\text{s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A loudspeaker, microphone and cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) are arranged as shown in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

Fig. 4.1

The loudspeaker is emitting a sound wave which is detected by the microphone and displayed on the screen of the CRO as shown in Fig. 4.2.

{{figure:figure_4_2}}

Fig. 4.2

The time-base on the CRO is set to $0.50\text{ ms cm}^{-1}$ and the $y$-gain is set to $0.20\text{ V cm}^{-1}$.

Calculate:

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: the frequency of the sound wave

markscheme_points.text: detail corresponding to first mark for (b)(i) as printed
detail corresponding to second mark for (b)(i) as printed

hints: Hint 1: Focus on the horizontal axis of Fig. 4.2. How many cm on the screen correspond to one complete sine wave cycle, and what does the time-base $0.50\text{ ms cm}^{-1}$ tell you about that length?
Hint 2: Once you have the time for one cycle, the period $T$, remember how period and frequency are inversely related and check your ms to s conversion.
parts.proper_answer: One cycle $= 4.0\text{ cm}$, $T = 4.0 \times 0.50\text{ ms} = 2.0\text{ ms} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$. $f = 1/T = 500\text{ Hz}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the period off the CRO**
The time-base tells you seconds per cm horizontally. Measure one full wavelength along the time axis in Fig. 4.2. You get about $4.0\text{ cm}$ per cycle. So $$T = \text{length of one cycle} \times \text{time-base}$$ $$T = 4.0 \times 0.50\text{ ms} = 2.0\text{ ms}$$

Step 2: **Convert to frequency**
Always convert ms to s before using $f = 1/T$: $$T = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$ $$f = \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 500\text{ Hz}$$ That is a sensible audio frequency.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: the amplitude of the signal received by the CRO.
hints: Hint 1: Remember amplitude is measured from the centre line to a peak, not peak-to-peak, and look at the vertical cm scale and the $0.20\text{ V cm}^{-1}$ y-gain.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Measure centre to peak**
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium, so on the CRO it is centre dashed line to top of crest. Here that is about $2.0\text{ cm}$. Then $$V_0 = \text{vertical height} \times \text{y-gain}$$ $$V_0 = 2.0 \times 0.20 = 0.40\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The intensity of the sound wave in (b) is reduced to a quarter of its original intensity without a change in frequency. Assume that the amplitude of the signal received by the CRO is proportional to the amplitude of the sound wave.

On Fig. 4.2, sketch the trace that is now seen on the screen of the CRO.

markscheme_points.text: of constant amplitude less than 2.8 cm throughout

hints: Hint 1: Start from the link between intensity and amplitude for a wave - if intensity drops to one quarter, does amplitude also drop to one quarter?
Hint 2: Think about what stays the same when only loudness changes - should the horizontal spacing of the peaks in Fig. 4.2 change?
Hint 3: Combine those ideas to picture the new trace - same shape and period as the original, but with what new centre-to-peak height in cm and volts?
parts.proper_answer: Intensity $\propto$ (amplitude)$^2$, so $I/4$ means amplitude$/2$. New amplitude $= 0.40/2 = 0.20\text{ V}$ ($1.0\text{ cm}$). Sketch same frequency trace as Fig. 4.2 with half the vertical height, constant amplitude throughout.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use intensity-amplitude law**
For any wave, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared: $$I \propto A^2$$ If $I$ becomes $I/4$, then $A^2$ becomes $A^2/4$, so $A$ becomes $A/2$. Halving is the key, not quartering.

Step 2: **Keep frequency the same**
The question says frequency is unchanged, so the period on the CRO is unchanged. Your sketch must line up peak-for-peak horizontally with the original trace in Fig. 4.2.

Step 3: **Draw the smaller trace**
Halve the vertical size: new centre-to-peak $= 1.0\text{ cm}$ corresponding to $0.20\text{ V}$. Draw a smooth sine wave of constant smaller amplitude over the whole screen, in phase with the original.

parts.label: (d)
parts.part_stem:
A metal sheet is now placed in front of the loudspeaker in (b), as shown in Fig. 4.3.

{{figure:figure_4_3}}

Fig. 4.3

A stationary wave is formed between the loudspeaker and the metal sheet.

parts.label: (d)(i)

markscheme_points.text: when (two or more) waves meet (at a point)
(resultant) displacement is the sum of the displacements

hints: Hint 1: Picture two waves arriving at the same point in air at the same instant - what two things does each wave bring to that point?
Hint 2: Think about how those individual disturbances combine to give what you actually observe - is it a multiplication, a subtraction, or an addition?
parts.proper_answer: When two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements of each wave.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Waves meeting**
Superposition only talks about the moment waves overlap in space. Here the forward wave from the loudspeaker meets the reflected wave from the metal sheet.

Step 2: **Add displacements**
At every instant the total disturbance is found by adding the displacements each wave would have alone, taking direction into account. That addition can give large antinodes where they reinforce and zero nodes where they cancel.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text:
The initial position of the microphone is such that the trace on the CRO has an amplitude minimum. It is now moved a distance of $1.05\text{ m}$ away from the loudspeaker along the line joining the loudspeaker and metal sheet.

As the microphone moves, it passes through three positions where the trace has an amplitude maximum before ending at a position where the trace has an amplitude minimum.

Determine the wavelength of the sound wave.

markscheme_points.text: microphone moves through 3 node-to-node or d = 1.5λ

hints: Hint 1: Recall what minimum and maximum amplitude mean on a stationary wave - which one is a node and how far apart are two neighbouring nodes?
Hint 2: Count carefully how many node-to-node gaps the microphone covers when it starts at a minimum, passes three maxima, and stops at the next minimum over $1.05\text{ m}$.
parts.proper_answer: Adjacent nodes (amplitude minima) are $\lambda/2$ apart. Distance $1.05\text{ m}$ contains 3 node-to-node intervals, so $1.05 = 3\lambda/2$, giving $\lambda = 0.70\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify nodes**
Amplitude minimum on the CRO means the microphone is at a node, amplitude maximum means at an antinode. In any stationary wave: $$\text{node to adjacent node} = \lambda/2$$

Step 2: **Count the intervals**
Start at node, then max-node-max-node-max-node. That is three full node-to-node steps. So $$1.05\text{ m} = 3 \times \frac{\lambda}{2} = 1.5\lambda$$ $$\lambda = \frac{1.05}{1.5} = 0.70\text{ m}$$

Hint 2: Count carefully how many node-to-node gaps the microphone covers when it starts at a minimum, passes three maxima, and stops at the next minimum over $1.05\text{ m}$.

parts.label: (d)(iii)
parts.text: Use your answers in (b)(i) and (d)(ii) to determine the speed of the sound in the air.
hints: Hint 1: You now have the two fingerprints of the sound wave - the frequency from the CRO in (b)(i) and the wavelength from the stationary wave in (d)(ii) - which universal wave relation links them to speed?
Hint 2: Plug the numbers in with correct units for $f$ in Hz and $\lambda$ in m to get $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choose the wave equation**
For any progressive wave, speed, frequency and wavelength are linked by $$v = f\lambda$$ Frequency was set by the loudspeaker and is unchanged by reflection, so use $f = 500\text{ Hz}$ from (b)(i).

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$v = 500 \times 0.70 = 350\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This is a very reasonable value for the speed of sound in air.
